records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page for the hybrid writes the binomial with an ASCII x ("Mentha x piperita"), while RHS's dedicated page (plant 11050) writes it with the multiplication sign ("Mentha × piperita") and gives its Name Status as Correct; it is recorded here with the multiplication sign. NC State describes the parentage as a cross between watermint (M. aquatica) and spearmint (M. spicata). Both dedicated pages lead with the same common name: NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list reads Peppermint, Peppermints, and RHS's page title reads "Mentha × piperita | peppermint", with brandy mint, lily-rail and lily-riall under its Other common names.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's "Problems" block for Mentha x piperita lists, in order: Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Weedy. These are tags only; no symptoms or severity are attached to them. The page's separate "Poisonous to Humans" block (human-scoped, not cat/dog-scoped) reads: Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: Vomiting and diarrhea with large ingestions; Poison Toxic Principle: Essential Oils; Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. The page banner says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." The page does not list a poisonous plant part. Plant Type on the page is Edible, Ground Cover, Herb, Herbaceous Perennial. Edibility statement: "Leaves and flowers can be used in tea and flavoring for various dishes." Description prose: "Use flowers and leaves fresh or dried in teas, beverages, jellies, syrups, candies, ice creams and mint sauce." No handling warning appears on the page. The "Weedy" tag and the advice to grow it in a 12-16" wide pot refer to aggressive spread, not size or toxicity. RHS's dedicated Mentha × piperita page (plant 11050) carries no toxicity or pet-hazard field, so no admissible source disagrees on scope; it files the plant under Herbs - Culinary, consistent with NC State's edibility statement.
unknowns: NC State's dedicated Mentha x piperita page and RHS's dedicated Mentha × piperita page (plant 11050) were both read. MoBot's Plant Finder page for the hybrid (taxonid 281400) fails TLS certificate verification from this machine, and Clemson HGIC's mint factsheet returns HTTP 403, so neither was read. RHS agrees with NC State on the common name (peppermint), sun (Position: Full sun, Partial shade) and drainage (Moisture: Moist but well–drained or Well–drained), and it carries no toxicity field. It differs on pH, where its pH field reads Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so NC State's 6.0-7.0 optimum is not landed as bounds. It also differs on spread: RHS gives Max Spread 1-1.5 metres (about 39-59 inches) and Max Height 0.5-1 metres (about 20-39 inches), against NC State's Width of 1-2 ft and Height of 1-3 ft. The record's size comes from NC State's Dimensions block.

is_houseplant landed false: no admissible source frames peppermint as a houseplant. NC State's USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field runs 5a-9b and its Landscape Theme field lists Cottage Garden, Edible Garden and Pollinator Garden; its pot advice ('Consider growing in a pot 12-16" wide to help control its aggressive spread.') confines an outdoor spreader, and RHS suggests Wildlife gardens and Cottage and informal garden.

Temperature, humidity, indoor light (foot-candles), fertilizing, and watering cadence are null: neither NC State nor RHS gives values for them, and RHS's H7 hardiness rating is not a damage-onset temperature. NC State's 'prefers rich moist soil' is a soil adjective, not a watering statement, and the 'wet soil' entry in its Particularly Resistant To (Insects/Diseases/Other Problems) field, which reads 'deer, rabbit, wet soil', is a tolerance trait, so water_regime is left null rather than set to keep_moist.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: the prose gives only 'a minimum of three hours of sun a day', which is a floor, and the 2-6 hour and 6+ hour figures are the site-wide light-category legend.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists full sun and partial shade; partial shade is mapped to part_shade. The tags 'full sun tolerant' and 'partial shade tolerant' agree. The prose says it prefers partial shade.

Soil pH: NC State's prose says 'It does best in neutral soils of 6.0-7.0 pH.', its structured Soil pH field reads 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)', and RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'. Because RHS lists both acid and alkaline soils as acceptable, neither 6.0 nor 7.0 is landed as a bound; 6.0-7.0 is NC State's stated best range, not a tolerance limit. The same NC State prose says the plant is tolerant of various soils except dry ones.

soil_base garden_bed is inferred from the in-ground culture language and Soil Texture field (Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt)); NC State also lists Container as a Landscape Location, and the page advises a 12-16 inch wide pot to confine spread.
soil_drainage is moderate: the structured field spans Good Drainage, Moist and Occasionally Wet, and the prose states only a preference for rich moist soil, so it is not moisture_retentive.

The Weedy tag and the 12-16 inch pot advice describe spread control, not mature size. Size comes from the Dimensions block (Height 1-3 ft, Width 1-2 ft). The separate Available Space To Plant field says 12 inches-3 feet and is not used.

NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Peppermint, Peppermints) and its order matches the page-title parenthetical. RHS's dedicated page agrees: its page title reads 'Mentha × piperita | peppermint', and its Other common names field reads 'brandy mint, lily-rail, lily-riall'.
NC State's page lists Mentha spicata and Nepeta x faassenii as often confused with this plant; nothing was borrowed from either.

is_edible is true for the leaves and flowers: NC State's Edibility field reads 'Leaves and flowers can be used in tea and flavoring for various dishes.' and its description adds 'Use flowers and leaves fresh or dried in teas, beverages, jellies, syrups, candies, ice creams and mint sauce.' The same page's human-scoped Poisonous to Humans block rates it Low severity, with Poison Symptoms 'Vomiting and diarrhea with large ingestions' and Essential Oils as the toxic principle, so the food use carries that large-ingestion caution; its Problems field separately lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses (see toxicity_detail).

records.name_note: NC State and RHS differ on the hybrid sign. NC State titles its page 'Thymus x citriodorus' (written here with the multiplication sign), but its own description says the plant 'at one time was thought to be a hybrid' and that 'DNA testing has now determined it to be a distinct species.' RHS's profile is headed 'Thymus citriodorus ambig.' with Name Status 'Correct' and shows no hybrid sign. The hybrid sign is kept following NC State's title. Both dedicated pages lead with the common name lemon thyme (NC State: 'Lemon Thyme'; RHS subtitle: 'lemon thyme'). NC State's Previously known as field lists Thymus citriodorus, Thymus fragrantissimus and Thymus serpyllum citratus.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Edibility field reads: 'Leaves and flowers can be eaten raw in salads or cooked in various dishes'. The NC State page carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag, and no admissible source consulted names cats or dogs, so pet toxicity is unrecorded rather than 'safe'.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden's page for this taxon (plantfinder.mobot.org, taxonid=250328) could not be loaded: the host's TLS chain failed verification from this sandbox and the www.missouribotanicalgarden.org URL redirects to it, so no MoBot content is cited.
Other admissible domains (Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD, UGA) returned only multi-species or genus-level thyme pages, not a dedicated lemon thyme page, so none are cited.

RHS has two profiles: 'Thymus citriodorus ambig.' (96407, carries the cultural data) and 'Thymus citriodorus (Pers.) Schreb.' (290762, Name Status 'Correct' but no cultural data). Cultural data here comes only from the first; neither RHS page shows the hybrid sign, while NC State's title does and its prose says 'DNA testing has now determined it to be a distinct species.'

NC State's structured Height field reads '6 ft. 0 in. - 1 ft. 0 in.', an evident typo; the prose gives 6-12 inches and that is used for mature_height_in. RHS's Max Height is 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 inches) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres, a wider upper bound than NC State's 12 inches; the NC State figures are used as the anchor.
toxic_to_pets left null: NC State has no poison block or pet tag, RHS has no toxicity field, and no cat or dog statement was found.

is_houseplant landed false: no admissible source frames lemon thyme as a houseplant. NC State's USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field runs 5a-8b and its uses are outdoor landscape uses ('Use this plant as a ground cover, in rock gardens, in the front of the border, in an edible garden or in containers.'); its Landscape Location field (Container, Patio, Pool/Hardscape, Slope/Bank) lists containers and patios as outdoor placements.
outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field and RHS Position both give full sun only; NC State prose says 'full to partial sun', a looser statement not used to add part_sun.

soil_drainage left null: no admissible source states a sharp or sandy requirement. NC State says 'Lemon thyme prefers well-drained sandy or rocky soil in full to partial sun.' (a preference), its Soil Texture field lists Loam (Silt), Sand and Shallow Rocky, its Soil Drainage field lists Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry, and it warns 'Root rot will occur in too-moist soils.' RHS gives Moisture 'Well–drained' and Soil Types Chalk, Loam, Sand. The plant is dry-tolerant with no wet tolerance, but loam is accepted and sand is only preferred, so fast is not established; nothing supports moderate (no Moist or Occasionally Wet value, no 'moist but well-drained'). RHS's Cultivation line ('Won't tolerate wet or waterlogged conditions. Will tolerate drought and poor soils.') is not used: the same paragraph appears verbatim on RHS's Thymus pulegioides 'Goldentime' profile, so it is stock Thymus text, not lemon-thyme evidence.
soil_ph_min/max left null: RHS lists 'Alkaline or Neutral' with no numeric figures, and NC State gives no pH field.

water_regime and the watering fields left null: neither page frames a watering instruction; RHS's 'Well-drained' moisture field and drought tolerance describe soil and tolerance, not watering. No fertilizer, temperature, humidity, indoor light or chill-damage figures appear on the admissible pages.
soil_base 'garden_bed' is inferred from the in-ground landscape uses NC State lists; the page also lists containers.
No parent-species page was used for any field: nothing was taken from Thymus vulgaris (landed as Thyme) or from Thymus pulegioides.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead name. RHS's dedicated page gives runner bean as the common name in its page title ('Phaseolus coccineus | runner bean') and lists scarlet runner bean under Other common names. NC State's Common Name(s) list for Phaseolus coccineus is alphabetized, opens on Aztec Bean and includes both Runner Bean and Scarlet Runner Bean. Runner Bean, RHS's lead name, is used. NC State's list also includes Snap Bean, and its prose calls the plant Snap Beans, but Snap Bean is also in the Common Name(s) list of Phaseolus vulgaris, the species NC State lists as often confused with this one.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS's dedicated Phaseolus coccineus page, under its Potentially harmful field: "Raw pods/beans harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets (dogs): Raw pods/beans harmful if eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers". Its pet line names dogs only; no admissible source names cats. NC State's page header reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." and its Poisonous to Humans block (human-scoped, not a pet rating) gives Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "In large amounts, the raw or undercooked beans can cause severe nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Usually resolves within a few hours."; Poison Toxic Principle: "Trace amounts of phytohaemagglutinin, a lectin"; Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; Poison Part: Seeds (the only part listed). NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual, Edible, Perennial, Vegetable and Vine; its Edibility field reads "Edible green pods that turn purple. The edible flowers are mild and crunchy. Young leaves are also edible." and its Fruit Description reads "Edible green pods that turn purple. Pick beans when young (3 to 5 inches long). If left on the vine, they will develop into large tough pods." NC State scopes its hazard to raw or undercooked beans in large amounts, RHS's covers raw pods as well as raw beans, and neither source gives a cooking time. On handling, RHS advises gloves while NC State's Causes Contact Dermatitis field reads No; both are recorded as given. Edible is therefore conditional: do not eat raw pods or raw or undercooked beans, and keep raw pods/beans away from dogs.
unknowns: is_houseplant landed false: no admissible source frames runner bean as a houseplant. Indoor growing appears only as raising seedlings before planting out: NC State says 'You can start Snap Beans in pots 4 to 6 weeks before last frost and then plant outside.' and RHS's runner bean guide says 'Runner beans won’t survive frost, so for an early crop sow seeds indoors in late spring.'

is_edible is true on a condition: NC State's Edibility field says the green pods, the flowers and the young leaves are edible, and RHS says the plant's pods are edible, but RHS's Potentially harmful field says 'Raw pods/beans harmful if eaten.' and NC State's Poison Symptoms say 'In large amounts, the raw or undercooked beans can cause severe nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Usually resolves within a few hours.' (Poison Part: Seeds; principle: trace amounts of phytohaemagglutinin, a lectin). Do not eat raw pods or raw or undercooked beans; neither source gives a cooking time. NC State's poison block is human-scoped; the only pet scope is RHS's dogs line ('Pets (dogs): Raw pods/beans harmful if eaten'), with no cat statement.

Life cycle: NC State says that in frost-free climates the plant can be grown as a perennial but dies back to the ground at the first hint of frost; RHS says that in the UK it is grown as a summer annual.

soil_drainage is moderate from NC State's bare Good Drainage + Moist pair and RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well-drained'. RHS's Cultivation paragraph separately says 'moisture-retentive soil', a mild tension, so moisture_retentive was not chosen; the prose preference is not read as a wet-soil requirement.

water_regime keep_moist rests on RHS's runner bean growing guide: 'Runner beans are thirsty plants and crop best when their roots have plenty of moisture, so regular watering is usually required, especially once they start to flower and form pods.' NC State's 'consistently moist, organically rich, well drained soil' and RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained' are soil descriptors that agree with it but do not by themselves set a watering regime. No source gives a day interval or dry-down depth, so those fields are null; the guide adds that container plants need 'frequent and generous watering'.
soil pH left null: NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band is a closed band, and RHS lists pH as acid or alkaline or neutral, so neither a floor nor a ceiling is supported.

Mature size uses NC State's Dimensions block (8-12 ft = 96-144 in height, 3-5 ft = 36-60 in width). climbs is true: NC State's Climbing Method field reads Twining and its prose says to 'provide poles or other support for the plant to climb on', and RHS calls the species 'a green-leaved twining climber reaching 3m', so mature_height_in 96-144 is the vine's reach given support, not a free-standing height. RHS gives Max Height 2.5-4 metres (98.4-157.5 in) and Max Spread 1-1.5 metres (39.4-59.1 in), consistent with NC State.

No admissible source states a damage-onset temperature, day or night temperature ranges, humidity, indoor light or direct-sun hours, so those fields are null. NC State says it is frost tender and RHS's runner bean guide says 'Runner beans won’t survive frost'; neither is a damage-onset figure, and the guide's 'Keep in a warm, bright place at over 12°C (54°F).' is a germination condition, not a growing range. records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead name. RHS's two pages for this species lead with the common name broad bean: its plant profile renders the common-name subtitle "broad bean" beneath the H1 "Vicia faba", and its grow-your-own guide is headed "How to Grow Broad beans" and names the plant "Broad beans (Vicia faba)". NC State's Vicia faba page is headed by the scientific name; its alphabetized Common Name(s) list of ten names begins with Bell Bean and includes Broad Bean, Faba Bean and Fava Bean, and its Description opens "Faba bean or broad bean". RHS's profile lists English bean, European bean, field bean, horse bean and straight bean under Other common names. NC State's Description says two subspecies are grown: var. major (broad beans), with large seeds and grown as a vegetable for human consumption, and var. minor (horse beans or field beans), grown for feeding livestock. Broad Bean, the lead name on both RHS pages, is used here for the species. Fava Bean is an alternate from NC State's list, and Horse Bean and Field Bean are not used.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Vicia faba page (no cat or dog scoping anywhere on the page). Plant Type: Annual, Edible, Poisonous, Vegetable. Problems: Poisonous to Humans. The page header reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Under the Poisonous to Humans heading (a human-scoped block): Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: "Persons ingesting numerous seeds and having a genetic predisposition to favism may develop a blood disorder (hemolytic anemia) by eating the beans, or even by walking through a field where the plants are in flower." Poison Toxic Principle: Cyanogenic glycosides. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Flowers, Fruits. The Description adds: "Ingestion can be poisonous to some individuals. Inhalation of the pollen or ingestion of the seeds may cause favism, which is a severe anemia destroying red blood cells. This only occurs in cases of excessive consumption of the raw seed or breathing the pollen in people with a genetic disposition towards the disease." The two NC State statements differ in scope: the Symptoms field ties favism to eating the beans, with no raw qualifier, or to walking through a field in flower, while the Description limits it to excessive consumption of the raw seed or breathing the pollen. Edibility field: "Faba bean is widely grown for its nutritious seeds and pods. The dry, mature seeds are popular in dishes throughout the Middle East, Mediterranean countries, China and Ethiopia and in many other countries the green immature seeds and pods are eaten as a vegetable. It is also used in animal feed for pigs, horses, poultry and pigeons." The page describes the fruit as a pod ("The fruit is a narrowly oblong flattened pod up to 11 inches long containing up to 6 seeds."), so Fruits is both a listed poison part and an eaten part. RHS's grow-your-own guide says "Young immature pods can also be picked when only about 5cm (2in) long, for cooking and eating whole." and "The shoot tips are tasty steamed or stir-fried."; neither RHS page carries a toxicity statement. No admissible source gives cooking times.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the only toxicity evidence (NC State Poisonous to Humans block) is human-scoped and no admissible source names cats or dogs.

Edibility is conditional. NC State's Edibility field says the dry mature seeds and the green immature seeds and pods are eaten. The same page lists the plant as Poisonous, with Poison Severity Low under its human-scoped Poisonous to Humans heading. It lists Flowers and Fruits as the poison parts, and its fruit is the pod. Its Poison Symptoms field says people with a genetic predisposition to favism who eat numerous seeds may develop hemolytic anemia "by eating the beans, or even by walking through a field where the plants are in flower", with no raw qualifier. Its Description says favism, "a severe anemia destroying red blood cells", only occurs with excessive consumption of the raw seed or breathing the pollen in people with a genetic disposition towards the disease. RHS describes eating the beans, young pods cooked whole and shoot tips steamed or stir-fried, and carries no toxicity statement. No admissible source gives cooking times.

soil_drainage moderate was landed on the audit's verified reading of RHS's Vicia faba profile (the research record had left it null): its Cultivation says it 'Does best in a sunny, sheltered position with fertile, moist but well drained soil, though most soils will produce an adequate crop.' and its Moisture field reads 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained', this catalog's moderate. NC State's structured Soil Drainage field lists Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry and its Description says the plant 'prefers moist loams but is tolerant of clay and saline soils and once established, drought'; with clay and saline tolerance that is not fast, and no source asks for consistently wet soil. RHS's guide asks for 'rich, free-draining soil'.

soil_ph left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), open-ended at both ends, and RHS's Vicia faba profile reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so no floor or ceiling is supported.

water_regime left null: RHS says broad beans in the ground do not generally need regular watering unless in light, free-draining soil, with a soak at flowering; NC State gives no watering statement. Not a clean enum fit.

Temperature fields left null: NC State says temperatures in the 60s are ideal and daytime temperatures above the mid 70s may result in poor yield, but this is not stated as a day or night range or a damage onset.
mature_spread_in is RHS's Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in); NC State gives no spread, and its Available Space To Plant (12 inches-3 feet) is planting space, not a mature spread.

Three admissible dedicated pages were read: NC State's Vicia faba page, RHS's broad bean grow-your-own guide (a cultivation guide with no structured fields) and RHS's Vicia faba plant profile, whose structured fields give Position Full sun, Moisture Moist but well–drained or Well–drained, pH Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, Max Height 0.5-1 metres and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres. Clemson HGIC's fava beans page returned 403 to this machine, UF/IFAS's broad bean publication MV017 returned 410 (no longer available on Ask IFAS), and no MoBot page was found.

mature_height_in 24-72 is NC State's prose figure, "It is a stiffly erect plant that grows 2-6 feet tall"; NC State's page has no Dimensions block. RHS's Vicia faba profile gives a lower range, Max Height 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in), and its description gives upright stems "0.4 to 1.2m tall" (15.7-47.2 in). RHS's guide adds that dwarf varieties "only reach about 50cm (20in) tall". NC State, the anchor page for this species, is recorded.

No admissible source frames Vicia faba as a houseplant or gives humidity or foot-candle light levels; is_houseplant is landed false on that basis (NC State's Landscape Theme field lists Edible Garden and Pollinator Garden, and RHS suggests Cottage and informal garden, Patio and container plants and Wildlife gardens). The fertilize fields stay null: RHS's guide says "Broad beans usually get all the nutrients they need from the soil." and feeds only container-grown dwarf plants, from when the first flowers appear, with a high potassium liquid fertiliser such as tomato feed once a fortnight. That is a word cadence with no stated day count, month range or dilution strength.

The task brief calls Pyrus serotina the older synonym, but no admissible page I could read states that, so it is not asserted in name_note or scientific_name_accepted.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: NC State's page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag, and no admissible source read names cats or dogs. No seed-cyanide wording was borrowed from Malus or Prunus.

The description separately advises planting 10 to 15 feet apart and says the tree can grow larger than 20 feet depending on its root stock graft, and the Available Space To Plant field says 24-60 feet. The structured range is landed and the spacing and rootstock caveat stay in prose.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists both 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', and the description says the tree prefers full sun. Partial Shade is mapped to part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour figures on the page are the generic light-category legend.
soil_drainage is null: NC State shows only 'Good Drainage' with no moisture tag, and the prose says 'well-drained', which is a bare well-drained reading and ambiguous.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) bands. The Acid band is open-ended so it gives no floor. The closed top of Neutral cannot be checked against an RHS pH field because no RHS page was available.
soil_base is garden_bed on the strength of an in-ground tree with the prose 'They grow in a variety of soils but prefer well-drained fertile soil and full sun'.

water_regime and all watering fields are null: NC State gives no watering statement for this species. Drought is listed under Resistance To Challenges, which is a tolerance trait and not a watering instruction.

fertilize fields are null: the only fertilizer guidance on NC State's page is "After the tree bears fruit around the 3rd or 4th year, you can reduce the fertilizer amount. Avoid excess nitrogen which could make it susceptible to fire blight." It gives no interval, months or dilution strength.

chill_damage_f, day/night temperatures, humidity and light foot-candle fields are null: NC State gives a USDA Plant Hardiness Zone range (5a, 5b, 6a, 6b, 7a, 7b, 8a, 8b), which is not a damage-onset temperature, and states no temperature figure. Its description says "The Asian pear grows well in areas with mild winters because they do not need a long cold period." and advises "The trees should be planted 10 to 15 feet apart in a frost-free location. They should be planted in an area to minimize the effects of a late spring frost."

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field for this species reads Edible and Tree, its USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field gives 5a-8b, its Landscape Location field lists Lawn, and its description says the trees should be planted 10 to 15 feet apart in a frost-free location. No admissible source frames Pyrus pyrifolia as a houseplant.

Related cautions on NC State's page: "Fire blight is the main problem." and "Deer will browse the tree." Its Problems field lists Frequent Disease Problems, Frequent Insect Problems and Messy, and its description says "The Asian pear should ripen on the tree. It also says "Depending on the cultivar, the Asian pear tree can grow large and should not be planted near overhead wires."

NC State's dedicated Borago officinalis page renders a Common Name(s) list of six names in alphabetical order, beginning with Borage: Borage, Cool Tankard, Cover Crop, Starflower, Tailwort, Talewort. Its page title carries the same six names in the same order as a parenthetical, (Borage, Cool Tankard, Cover Crop, Starflower, Tailwort, Talewort). Its description prose opens on Starflower ("Starflower is an annual plant in the forget-me-not or Boraginaceae family ..."). NC State's list and its page title both lead with Borage; the description's opening sentence is the only place the NC State page leads with Starflower.
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, Borago officinalis page. Its Problems field lists Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses. The cat and dog entries are separate tags and are not part of the human-scoped Poison block. The page banner reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." The Poisonous to Humans block gives Poison Severity: Low, and that severity belongs to this human-scoped block. Poison Symptoms: "The plant contains toxins (PAs) that can damage the liver and lungs, and are potentially carcinogenic. Should only be used sparingly." Poison Toxic Principle: Tannins, mucilage. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Leaves. The page contradicts itself. The symptoms text names pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs) as the toxins, but the toxic-principle field names tannins and mucilage. The poison part is given as leaves only, although the edibility text also names flowers and borage seed oil. Causes Contact Dermatitis is No, yet the page's tags include #contact dermatitis. The page lists no symptom list for cats or dogs. Plant Type field: Annual, Edible, Herb. Full tag line: #blue flowers #full sun tolerant #pollinator plant #problem for cats #problem for dogs #problem for horses #deer resistant #drought tolerant #bee friendly #annual #poor soil tolerant #contact dermatitis #microgreens #wildlife friendly #th-sowing #th-taste #th-touch #th-smell #edible flowers. Edibility statement, with its conditions: the flowers (used as edible flowers) and leaves (used in salads, teas, and sandwiches) are edible in general, but "They should only be usred sparingly as liver damage can occur. Only use borage seed oil that is certified as PA-free." Missouri Botanical Garden's page could not be read from this machine, so no second source is compared here (see unknowns).
unknowns: EDIBILITY IS CONDITIONAL. is_edible is true, but NC State's Edibility field says the flowers and leaves 'should only be usred sparingly as liver damage can occur' and 'Only use borage seed oil that is certified as PA-free.', and its Poison Symptoms field says 'The plant contains toxins (PAs) that can damage the liver and lungs, and are potentially carcinogenic.
